name: Apache Iceberg
summary: The most widely supported open table format: snapshots of data files, tracked by a tree of metadata and swapped in atomically through a catalog.
intro: An Iceberg table is a tree of files. At the top, a table metadata file records the schema, the partition spec and the list of snapshots. Each snapshot points to a manifest list, which points to manifests, which list the data files (usually Parquet) with column statistics for each file. A catalog, such as a REST catalog, AWS Glue or a JDBC database, stores where the current metadata file is, and a commit swaps that pointer atomically.

Because there are statistics at every level, an engine can rule out whole manifests without listing any directories. Partitioning is hidden: you partition by `days(ts)`, queries just filter on `ts`, and you can change the scheme later without rewriting old data. Netflix built Iceberg and contributed it to the Apache Software Foundation in 2018. Spec versions 1, 2 and 3 are complete; v3 adds deletion vectors, row lineage, column default values and new types such as `variant`, geometry and nanosecond timestamps. Version 4 is still in development.
strengths: Wide engine support: Spark, Flink, Trino, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena and Redshift all work with it
The REST catalog protocol is an open standard, so one catalog can serve every engine
Hidden partitioning and partition evolution avoid accidental full scans and painful re-partitioning
Managed offerings on the big clouds, such as Amazon S3 Tables and Google’s Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery
limits: You need a catalog, and choosing one (Glue, Polaris, Nessie, a JDBC database and others) is a real decision
Frequent small commits pile up snapshots, manifests and small files, so compaction and snapshot expiry must run on a schedule
Engines adopt new spec versions unevenly: Athena works only with v2 tables, and Trino’s v3 support is experimental
Many concurrent writers to one table cause commit conflicts and retries

story: Netflix ran its analytics on Hive tables, the de facto standard layout that Hive, Presto and Spark all used. A Hive table tracks its partitions in a central metastore and finds the files inside by listing directories. On S3 that listing is slow, and while S3 listings were eventually consistent it could return wrong results. Changes to a table couldn’t be atomic, object stores have no real rename, and the metastore became a bottleneck when planning jobs.

Ryan Blue and Dan Weeks started Iceberg at Netflix in 2017 as “a new table format for storing large, slow-moving tabular data”, one that tracks every data file instead of directories. Netflix donated it to the Apache Software Foundation, where it entered the incubator in November 2018 and graduated in May 2020. Blue, Weeks and Jason Reid later founded Tabular, a data management company built on Iceberg.

Iceberg became the format most engines agreed on. In June 2024 Databricks, the company behind rival Delta Lake, agreed to acquire Tabular with the aim of making the two formats compatible, and in December 2024 AWS launched S3 Tables, which builds Iceberg support into S3 itself.

choices.why: Listing partition paths was slow on S3 and gave no atomicity. Iceberg’s metadata names every data file, so writers create files where they like and commit them explicitly, and planning a scan needs no listing.
Each change writes new metadata, then atomically replaces the pointer to the current metadata file. Readers never take locks and never see a partial write: the spec’s goal is serializable isolation.

choices.choice: A written spec, independent of any engine
choices.why: Hive’s layout was a convention built into each engine. Iceberg wrote the table format down as a specification, so Spark, Trino, Flink and others could each implement it and read the same tables.

choices.choice: Schema and partition changes are metadata-only
choices.why: The spec requires safe add, drop, rename and reorder of columns, including nested ones, and partition spec evolution, so changing a table’s design never means rewriting old data.

timeline.text: Ryan Blue and Dan Weeks start Iceberg at Netflix
Donated to the Apache Software Foundation; enters the incubator in November
Graduates to a top-level Apache project in May
Format v2 tables, with row-level deletes, arrive in Iceberg 0.12
Databricks agrees to buy Tabular (June); AWS launches S3 Tables (December)
Iceberg 1.8 adds format v3 features: deletion vectors, `variant`, row lineage
